patterns.summary: All four add a noun wherever the Greek uses a neuter adjective, pronoun, or article: 'subjects', 'premises', 'things', 'matters', 'points'. They agree that a noun is needed but rarely on which one.
patterns.translators: All four; Ostwald and Rackham add the most such nouns, Peters the fewest.

patterns.summary: Rackham adds whole phrases the Greek does not state: 'this science', 'Moral', 'real existence', 'these conceptions', 'Moral Science' for 'knowing about these'. These are the hardest to link to any Greek word.
Connecting particles (δέ, γάρ, δή, καί, μέν) often get no English. Ross keeps them most often as 'now', 'for', 'and'; no one renders γάρ in 1094b26 or the 'also' before 'conclude'.
patterns.translators: Ostwald and Peters omit most; Ross least.

patterns.summary: Impersonal and passive Greek turns personal: 'it is welcome' becomes 'we must be content', 'it seems' becomes 'some people believe', and datives of the person become the subject.
patterns.translators: Peters and Ostwald most; Ross least.

patterns.summary: Key terms get a fixed word per translator: πλάνη is uncertainty, fluctuation, or irregularity; πάθος is feeling, passion, or emotion; πολιτική is 'political science' (Rackham, Ross) or 'politics' (Ostwald, Peters). Only ἀκριβές drifts within one version (Peters: precision, accuracy, exactness).
Where the Greek leaves out a verb or predicate already stated, all four repeat it: 'a good judge' in 1095a1, 'any more than it can be expected' in 1094b14, 'it is enough if' in 1094b21.
patterns.translators: All four in 1095a1; elsewhere Ostwald and Rackham most, Ross least.

patterns.summary: Rackham and Peters move the sentence frame: Rackham turns a relative clause into a main clause and makes causes into subjects; Peters splits a sentence mid-clause (1094b28) and reverses the order of 'young in years' and 'young in character'.
patterns.translators: Peters and Rackham most; Ross and Ostwald least.
